newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain pledges to win back market confidence.
newsitem.headline: Spain pledges to win back market confidence.

text.p: Just five weeks after he threw financial markets into disarray with the discovery of a yawning 1995 budget gap, Spain's Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato vowed on Tuesday to restore confidence in the nation's fiscal discipline.

Rato, speaking to Congress, detailed financing to plug the 721 billion peseta ($5.7 billion) shortfall which conservatives said they inherited from the former Socialist government. He also promised a law to prevent a repetition of the debacle.

"These are grave, crucial situations -- but by no means unique in Spanish budgetary history," Rato said. "We will present a bill that will make it impossible for a situation such as the one we are now facing to ever reoccur."
The government said the shortfall stemmed mainly from items for which the Socialists, dislodged in March after 13 years in power, neither budgeted nor paid.
Almost half of the shortfall turned up in the accounts of the Public Works Ministry, but gaps were also found in the Ministries of Agriculture, Justice and Interior.

To compensate, the government announced a hike on taxes in cigarettes and alcohol which took effect in August. Rato said he expects the new taxes to generate receipts of 30 billion pesetas this year and of 75 billion in 1997.
In addition, the government will issue extra debt and Rato forecast interest expense of some 40 billion pesetas annually, with added funds needed to pay off the principal amount.
"This news (of the gap) prompted a loss of credibility in the process of budgetary adjustment in Spain," Rato said.

"The only way to restore credibility in the budget process and in the success of the convergence programme is to take these two steps," he added, referring to the funding to patch the hole and a law to prevent a repetition.
The stakes are high. The government's 1997 budget -- on which rest Spain's hopes to join the launch of the European single currency -- is due by the end of the month.

The government's thorniest problem is reducing the deficit to gross domestic product ratio to the three percent threshhold required for participation in the Euro's launch, from a projected 4.4 percent this year.
The unexpected 1995 shortfall forced that year's ratio to 6.6 percent from the 5.9 percent level originally expected.

The market has already recovered considerably from the shock, with the spread of Spanish bond yields to their German counterparts back to where they were before the added deficit risk bloated them, Rato said.
The improvement stemmed largely from a recovery in recent budget deficit data.
Spain had a surplus of 282.1 billion pesetas in July, paring the year-to-date deficit down to 1.18 trillion pesetas. ($1=125.6 Peseta)
